title: How Porn Sites Learned to Create Addictive Content Using Click Data—Before Big Tech
dek: In the 1990s, pornographic content pioneered free access, user-generated content, and data-driven creation; this logic of ‘reverse-engineering content from clicks’ later became the underlying template for the entire internet platform economy.
why: The cases are solid and the argument is clear, but the second half's discussion of chatbots and intimate relationships sprawls somewhat; if you want to understand why algorithms favor extreme content, this episode is worth listening to.
who: Product managers and creators who want to understand why algorithms always push extreme content and care about how content platform business models have evolved.

points.h: Porn director's rebuttal: you're the perverts
points.body: At a pornography industry party in Prague, a director who specializes in humiliation content pushed back emotionally: he didn't personally find the material arousing—he filmed it only because the data showed audiences clicked on it. That moment made the author realize that content direction isn't determined by platform malice, but by what audiences themselves can't articulate yet can't resist clicking.

points.h: Free pornography started with stolen content
points.body: The shift from paid DVDs and magazines to free online content wasn't driven by traditional porn moguls but by early programmers and website administrators. Most of this content was stolen without performers' consent, and it was these same technologists—the first to explore how to monetize the internet through ads and traffic—not the porn industry itself, who built the first successful ad-driven business model around it.

points.h: Porn sites invented livestreaming and online payments before Big Tech
points.body: Many internet technologies taken for granted were first pioneered in the porn industry: mid-1990s camming sites essentially invented real-time video interaction; early online payment systems also relied heavily on sex worker and pornography transactions—a former Visa executive she interviewed disclosed that at the time, as much as 10% to 15% of online transactions were sex-related.

points.h: Mobile and ad-blocking forced data-driven creation into existence
points.body: Around 2010, as users migrated to mobile and started using ad-blockers, the model of pulling new users with banner ads collapsed. Platforms had to pivot to studying user behavior data to improve retention. By 2019, Pornhub's parent company was recognized as the industry leader in ‘data-driven creation’—reverse-engineering content from user clicks, dwell time, and return visits to produce the most addictive possible material. This model was later adopted by Amazon, Spotify, and every major content platform.

points.h: Algorithms favor extreme content; political polarization operates on the same principle
points.body: Infinite-scroll porn sites chase intensity and novelty, so niche BDSM, humiliation, and domination content gradually became ‘mainstream’ pornography—now visible in young people's actual sexual behavior. The author further argues that understanding political polarization requires the same logic: the domination and humiliation narratives around Andrew Tate and even Trump are exactly the material that algorithms have already tested and verified in pornography as most triggering to users.

points.h: Prague's porn industry runs on undocumented migrant women
points.body: Before the war, many female performers in Prague's humiliation porn came from Russia and Ukraine, where pornography production is illegal. They were flown to Prague under the guise of ‘tourism’ but couldn't report crimes because they lacked EU work permits. The author emphasizes that once discussion becomes purely about ‘content’, it's easy to forget the unprotected real people behind the screen.

points.h: OnlyFans customers demand self-harm to prove authenticity
points.body: Multiple OnlyFans and livestream performers the author interviewed mentioned that customers had asked them to self-harm. One performer believed customers wanted something that would ‘leave marks’—scars persist on the body after the camera stops, and that permanence made customers feel the interaction was ‘real’ rather than just performance.

points.h: OnlyFans sex chat is actually outsourced to ghost writers
points.body: Performers can't chat with hundreds of thousands of followers simultaneously, so the ‘flirting’ work is outsourced to chat workers in places like the Philippines at as low as $1 per hour, with compensation based on tips or content purchases they generate. Even when users know it might not be the performer, the interaction still ‘feels more real’, and the author argues that this trained parasocial intimacy is exactly why people so easily form emotional dependencies with AI chatbots.
